Reconcile forecast draws over a hierarchy

Source: R/hierarchy.R
mt_reconcile.Rd

Makes forecasts of nested or crossed strata add up, draw by draw. For each age, year and draw, the base forecasts y of all strata in the hierarchy (bottom series and aggregates) are projected onto the coherent subspace, y - W U (U' W U)^-1 U' y, where U' y = 0 are the aggregation constraints (each aggregate equals the sum of its bottom series). With additive = "deaths" in the hierarchy, the projection works on expected deaths (rates times exposures; exposures of aggregates are the sums of their bottom series), and reconciled rates are reconciled deaths divided by exposures. Methods choose W:

Usage

mt_reconcile(
  draws,
  hierarchy = NULL,
  method = c("wls", "mint", "structural", "ols", "bottom_up", "proportional"),
  shrink = "auto",
  exposure = NULL,
  dependence = c("none", "schaake", "empirical"),
  seed = NULL,
  fixed = NULL,
  var = NULL,
  total = NULL,
  parts = NULL
)

Arguments

draws

An mt_draws object with the strata of the hierarchy.

hierarchy

An mt_hierarchy() (or, for one variable, var and total).

method

"wls" (default), "mint", "structural", "ols", "bottom_up" or "proportional" (with fixed). The vignette "Coherent forecasts: totals and their parts" compares them. Score-optimal reconciliation ("energy_score") is learnt from past forecasts and is available in reconciled() only.

shrink

Shrinkage intensity for "mint" (number between 0 and 1), or "auto".

exposure

Exposures [age, period, stratum] or [age, stratum] for the forecast years (default: last training year). Only bottom strata are used, and they are enough; aggregates are summed.

dependence

"none" (default: keep the draws as they are), "schaake" (the Schaake shuffle of every age, year and stratum of the draws of separately fitted strata before the reconciliation) or "empirical" (the Schaake shuffle of the whole paths of each stratum); see Details. Draws of joint models are not reordered: both then give a warning and are ignored. Both need the training data of the draws (as mt_forecast() returns them); "schaake" needs at least two more training years than forecast years, "empirical" at least three training years.

seed

Random seed for the Schaake shuffle (order of the draws, choice of dates, ties).

fixed

Strata whose forecasts are kept unchanged (labels, or "total" for the grand total of the hierarchy), for example a trusted all-cause forecast that the causes must add up to. The projection gives these nodes near-zero variance, so the other strata absorb the whole gap; $reconciliation$max_relative_change_fixed reports how closely they were kept; they move, with a warning, when their own forecasts do not add up (a node fixed together with all its parts) or when every bottom stratum below them would have to be negative. Needs a projection method or "proportional".

var, total, parts

One-variable form: stratum variable and its total level (parts is ignored: all other levels are parts).

Value

The reconciled mt_draws, with diagnostics in $reconciliation (method, largest relative gap before reconciliation, share of bottom values held at zero, mean shrinkage intensity). After the Schaake shuffle, $schaake holds the number of dates (dates), their start years (years), the start year of the date of each draw (draw_year), the block of each draw (block), the number of blocks (blocks), the number of shuffled margins (margins) and the share of margins with tied template values (tied); $component is then dropped, since the values of one draw come from different base draws. After the shuffle of stratum paths, $empirical holds the same items, with the years of the observed changes as years and the number of reordered strata as margins, and also the standard population (standard) and the template (template, the observed annual changes of the log age-standardised rate [stratum, year]); $component then gives the component of each stratum and draw (ensembles).

Details

  • "ols": identity (Hyndman, Ahmed, Athanasopoulos and Shang 2011);

  • "structural": diagonal with the number of bottom series in each node (structural scaling, Athanasopoulos, Hyndman, Kourentzes and Petropoulos 2017);

  • "wls": diagonal with the variance of each stratum's base draws (weighted least squares, Hyndman, Lee and Wang 2016; see below);

  • "mint": covariance of the base draws across strata, shrunk towards its diagonal with the intensity of Schäfer and Strimmer (2005) by default (minimum-trace reconciliation, Wickramasuriya, Athanasopoulos and Hyndman 2019; see below);

  • "bottom_up": aggregates are the sums of the bottom forecasts.

W of "wls" and "mint". In the papers, W holds the variances (Hyndman, Lee and Wang 2016) or the shrunk covariance matrix (Wickramasuriya et al. 2019) of the in-sample one-step-ahead residuals of the base models. Here W is the variance ("wls") or the Schäfer-Strimmer shrunk covariance ("mint") of the base forecast draws across draws, computed separately in each age and forecast year cell: the variance of the model's own h-step forecast of that cell (of expected deaths, or of rates when the levels share exposures; without the Poisson variation of the deaths unless predictive draws are reconciled). It changes with the horizon and follows the uncertainty the model reports, not its past errors: a stratum whose model is too narrow is changed too little. For strata fitted by separate models the base draws are independent across strata, so the shrunk covariance is close to its diagonal and "mint" gives nearly the result of "wls"; it differs where a joint model (for example li_lee()) simulates correlated strata, or after the Schaake shuffle. reconciled() with covariance = "errors" estimates W from the errors of past forecasts instead, the input of the papers.

Non-negative forecasts. Projections can make bottom values negative where the base forecasts disagree strongly. For the draws where this happens, the bottom values b are those of the non-negative reconciliation of Wickramasuriya, Turlach and Hyndman (2020): they minimise the same weighted distance (y - S b)' W^-1 (y - S b) subject to b >= 0 (their Eq. 3), and the aggregates are their sums. The quadratic program is solved exactly by their block principal pivoting algorithm (their Algorithm 3.1: all infeasible values exchanged while their number falls, at most 3 times without a fall, then one value at a time), started from the unconstrained solution, with the projection above for each set of bottom values held at zero. Infeasibilities below 1e-10 times the largest absolute base forecast of the draw count as zero (the paper uses 1e-12 in absolute terms). Draws without negative values keep the unconstrained solution, which is then the optimum. A warning reports when more than 5% of the draws have bottom values at zero, because the distributions of the affected strata (often small causes) are then truncated at zero. Earlier versions of mortensor held negative values at zero and projected the rest again, a heuristic without a guaranteed optimum; it was removed.

Fixed nodes. fixed keeps the forecasts of some nodes, as in the reconciliation with immutable forecasts of Zhang, Kang, Panagiotelis and Li (2023). The package gives the fixed nodes a near-zero variance in W (1e-10 times the largest variance); with "mint" the other nodes get their covariance conditional on the fixed nodes. The projection is then the weighted least-squares solution with the fixed nodes as equality constraints, up to a relative change of the fixed nodes of about 1e-9, and the other strata absorb the whole gap. With negative bottom values, the same weights enter the non-negative quadratic program, so the fixed nodes are kept as equality constraints there as well, as long as non-negative parts can add up to them. When they cannot (a fixed node below zero, or a node fixed together with parts whose forecasts do not add up to it), the fixed nodes move, with a warning.

Proportional. "proportional" keeps the fixed nodes and scales the bottom strata below each of them by one factor per draw, so that they add up to the fixed node; nodes between them are recomputed as sums. This is a single-level top-down method (Gross and Sohl 1990) with forecast proportions (Athanasopoulos, Ahmed and Hyndman 2009): the proportions are those of the bottom forecasts below the fixed node in the same draw, while Athanasopoulos et al. (2009) derive them level by level down the hierarchy (the same for two levels). It never sets a part to zero. Fixed nodes must not share parts.

Dependence between strata. Strata forecast by separate models have independent draws. With dependence = "none" (default), the draws are reconciled as they are, so sums of separately fitted parts have narrower intervals than they would if the parts moved together. Joint models (for example li_lee(), coherent_fdm() and coda() with coherent = TRUE) carry the dependence between strata in the model itself; their draws are never reordered ("schaake" and "empirical" then give a warning and are ignored). Three methods give separately fitted strata a dependence before the reconciliation, all by reordering their draws. The Schaake shuffle takes the dependence from the observed changes of the training years, either in every age, forecast year and stratum (dependence = "schaake") or for the whole path of each stratum (dependence = "empirical"), both below. Ensemble copula coupling (Schefzik, Thorarinsdottir and Gneiting 2013) takes it from the draws of a joint model (mt_couple() for draws before mt_reconcile(), and coupled() or reconciled(dependence = "ecc") for models).

The Schaake shuffle (dependence = "schaake"; Clark, Gangopadhyay, Hay, Rajagopalan and Wilby 2004, Section 3b). Status: published, adapted to mortality forecasts as listed below. In the paper, the ensemble members of each station and variable are reordered so that their ranks follow those of observations from as many dates of the historical record, the same dates for all stations and variables (their eqs. 5-12); the later lead times take the following days of the same dates, which keeps the persistence over lead times. Here a margin is an age, a forecast year and a stratum. The template value of a date, a training year tau, for the margin of forecast year h (counted from the last training year) is the observed change of the log death rate from tau to tau + h: one observed trajectory per date, over consecutive years. The dates are the n training years whose next H years are observed (H the number of forecast years, so n is the number of training years minus H), from the training data of the draws only. In every margin the draws receive the sorted values of that margin in the rank order of the template values of their dates. Every margin keeps exactly its values, and the draws take the rank correlations of the observed changes between strata, between ages and between forecast years. Ties among template values are ranked at random, as in the paper (Section 4c); margins with a missing template value keep the order of their draws, as the paper's code skips vectors with missing values (appendix), with a warning. Schefzik et al. (2013, Section 3.4) describe the shuffle as the empirical copula of the historical record applied to samples of the margins; ensemble copula coupling takes the copula from the draws of a model instead.

Package-specific (reference unknown): (1) the template holds changes of log rates from the start year of each date, where the paper takes the observed values themselves (from dates within seven days of the forecast date), so that the ranks follow the variation of past changes around the trend of mortality; (2) deaths of zero count as 0.5 in the template; (3) the paper has as many dates as ensemble members. With more draws than dates, the draws are taken in a random order in blocks of n, and each block is shuffled with all n dates; a last block with fewer draws uses a random subset of distinct dates, as do fewer draws than dates (the paper selects its dates at random). The draws of a block take the ranks of the template among themselves, and the same dates recur in every block.

The shuffle assumes that the dependence of the training years holds in the forecast years (Clark et al. 2004, Section 5). It sets the dependence between the ages and years of a stratum as well, so measures over ages, such as the life expectancy of a single stratum, change: Lee-Carter draws move all ages of a stratum together, and after the shuffle they move together as much as the observed changes did, which narrows the intervals of life expectancy where these are less correlated between ages. The observed changes carry the Poisson variation of the deaths, which is independent between strata and ages; where deaths are few, it weakens the dependence the template gives. Templates are short: with 19 training years and 5 forecast years there are 14 dates, with 16 forecast years 3.

The Schaake shuffle of stratum paths (dependence = "empirical"). Status: the Schaake shuffle of Clark et al. (2004, Section 3b) with the stratum as margin; the margin and the summary that ranks the paths are package-specific (see below). The path of a stratum in one draw, all its ages and forecast years, is one ensemble member and is moved as a whole. The members of each stratum are ranked by a summary of their path, and they are reordered so that their ranks follow those of the same summary in the observed data of n distinct training years (the dates), the same dates for all strata, as in the paper. Every stratum keeps exactly its set of paths: its forecast distribution and the dependence between its ages and years stay those of the model, and with method = "bottom_up" so do all scores of the bottom strata (reconciled() keeps this for predictive draws as well). The pairing of the paths of different strata changes, so that strata whose summaries moved together in the same training years move together in the forecast. In the terms of Schefzik et al. (2013, Section 3.4), the summaries of the strata take the empirical copula of their observed changes. Ben Taieb, Taylor and Hyndman (2021) reorder samples of the bottom series of a hierarchy in the same way, with the empirical copula of in-sample residuals, and sum them bottom-up; Panagiotelis, Gamakumara, Athanasopoulos and Hyndman (2023, Sections 1 and 7.3) discuss that method and note that it needs as many draws as training observations.

The summary is the log age-standardised death rate z, with one standard population for all strata: the mean exposure of each age over the strata and training years of the draws, so that ages enter with their weight in the population. The template value of a stratum and training year tau is the observed annual change z[tau] - z[tau - 1], so n is the number of training years minus one. A draw is ranked by the mean annual change of its summary over the forecast years, (z[H] - z[0]) / H, where z[H] is the summary in the last forecast year and z[0] that of the observed rates of the last training year. Both ranks so refer to annual changes of the summary; z[0] is the same for all draws of a stratum, so the ranks of the draws are those of z[H]. Draws and dates are matched in blocks as for "schaake" (item 3 above); ties among template values are ranked at random (Clark et al. 2004, Section 4c); deaths of zero count as 0.5. With fewer than three training years (one observed change) the draws keep their order, with a warning. A stratum with a missing template value keeps the order of its draws, with a warning.

Package-specific (reference unknown): the stratum as margin, the summary and its standard population, the ranking of the draws by their mean annual change, and the blocks with more draws than dates.

The three methods differ in what they reorder. "schaake" reorders every age, forecast year and stratum separately: it replaces the dependence between the ages and years of a stratum with that of the observed changes as well, which changes measures over ages and years of a single stratum (life expectancy, cumulative changes). "empirical" leaves each stratum to its model and gives only the strata a dependence, from one summary per stratum and year, which carries less Poisson variation than the rates of single ages. "ecc" takes the dependence of all cells from the draws of a joint model, in place of observed years. Each assumes that the dependence it takes holds in the forecast years. The template of "empirical" holds the changes of single years, and the draws are ranked by their changes over all forecast years: the strata of one draw take the ranks that their annual changes had in one training year, so they move together as far as their annual changes did. The observed changes carry the Poisson variation of the deaths, which is independent between strata and weakens the dependence where deaths are few.

In the package's backtests of bottom-up Lee-Carter forecasts, on data simulated with correlated period shocks, on the deprivation quintiles of England (ons_data) and on the German Laender, "empirical" widened the intervals of the totals towards their nominal coverage and lowered their CRPS, with the scores of every stratum unchanged; on mt_example_regions(), whose separate forecasts already covered the totals, it made the intervals of the totals too wide. The vignettes "Coherent forecasts: totals and their parts" and "Dependence between groups" show such backtests.

The one-variable interface with var and total is still accepted. It reconciles deaths when the exposures of the parts add up to that of the total (sexes, regions) and rates when each part has the exposure of the total (causes of death) or there are no exposures; give a hierarchy with additive to choose.

References

Hyndman RJ, Ahmed RA, Athanasopoulos G, Shang HL (2011). Optimal combination forecasts for hierarchical time series. Computational Statistics & Data Analysis 55(9): 2579-2589.

Hyndman RJ, Lee AJ, Wang E (2016). Fast computation of reconciled forecasts for hierarchical and grouped time series. Computational Statistics & Data Analysis 97.

Athanasopoulos G, Hyndman RJ, Kourentzes N, Petropoulos F (2017). Forecasting with temporal hierarchies. European Journal of Operational Research 262(1): 60-74.

Wickramasuriya SL, Athanasopoulos G, Hyndman RJ (2019). Optimal forecast reconciliation for hierarchical and grouped time series through trace minimization. Journal of the American Statistical Association 114(526): 804-819. doi:10.1080/01621459.2018.1448825

Wickramasuriya SL, Turlach BA, Hyndman RJ (2020). Optimal non-negative forecast reconciliation. Statistics and Computing 30: 1167-1182. doi:10.1007/s11222-020-09930-0

Zhang B, Kang Y, Panagiotelis A, Li F (2023). Optimal reconciliation with immutable forecasts. European Journal of Operational Research 308(2): 650-660. doi:10.1016/j.ejor.2022.11.035

Gross CW, Sohl JE (1990). Disaggregation methods to expedite product line forecasting. Journal of Forecasting 9(3): 233-254.

Athanasopoulos G, Ahmed RA, Hyndman RJ (2009). Hierarchical forecasts for Australian domestic tourism. International Journal of Forecasting 25: 146-166.

Clark M, Gangopadhyay S, Hay L, Rajagopalan B, Wilby R (2004). The Schaake shuffle: a method for reconstructing space-time variability in forecasted precipitation and temperature fields. Journal of Hydrometeorology 5(1): 243-262.

Schefzik R, Thorarinsdottir TL, Gneiting T (2013). Uncertainty quantification in complex simulation models using ensemble copula coupling. Statistical Science 28(4): 616-640. doi:10.1214/13-STS443

Panagiotelis A, Gamakumara P, Athanasopoulos G, Hyndman RJ (2023). Probabilistic forecast reconciliation: properties, evaluation and score optimisation. European Journal of Operational Research 306(2): 693-706. doi:10.1016/j.ejor.2022.07.040

Schäfer J, Strimmer K (2005). A shrinkage approach to large-scale covariance matrix estimation and implications for functional genomics. Statistical Applications in Genetics and Molecular Biology 4(1): Article 32. doi:10.2202/1544-6115.1175

Examples

x <- mt_example_regions(years = 2005:2019, regions = 3)
h <- mt_hierarchy(sex = "both", region = "all", quintile = "all")
xa <- mt_aggregate_strata(x, h)
fc <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(lee_carter(), xa), h = 3, n_draws = 50, seed = 1)
rc <- mt_reconcile(fc, h, method = "wls")
rc$reconciliation
#> $method
#> [1] "wls"
#> 
#> $max_relative_gap_before
#> [1] 0.9210924
#> 
#> $share_set_to_zero
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> $mean_shrinkage
#> [1] NA
#> 
#> $share_draws_with_zeros
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> $max_relative_change_fixed
#> [1] NA
#> 
# the strata take the dependence of the observed changes of 12 training years
rs <- mt_reconcile(fc, h, method = "wls", dependence = "schaake", seed = 1)
rs$schaake$years
#>  [1] 2005 2006 2007 2008 2009 2010 2011 2012 2013 2014 2015 2016
# whole paths of each stratum, ranked by the annual changes of 14 training years
re <- mt_reconcile(fc, h, method = "bottom_up", dependence = "empirical", seed = 1)
re$empirical$template[1:3, 1:5]
#>               year
#> stratum              2006         2007        2008         2009         2010
#>   female.R1.Q1 0.00100760  0.004208635 -0.01625161 -0.007325809 -0.007361821
#>   female.R1.Q2 0.01916212  0.003678371 -0.01387691  0.001738056 -0.001813413
#>   female.R1.Q3 0.02737474 -0.013021711 -0.02361212  0.015747796 -0.001853880
